This is an interesting hacking game and it does get the basic points across (i.e. explore stuff, avoid red herrings and all) but the "hacking" commands are way way simplified to the point that it becomes repetitive...

I think the beauty in hacking (games) mostly comes from having to think outside the box and deduce what the system "might be doing" by observing its outward behavior and exploiting that knowledge to come up with weaknesses to then attack or try attacking. Having a command to execute to just "script everything" takes all the fun out of things. 

Looking at this as an introductory game, it then seems too contrived with the aesthetic of  the command line and weird GUI etc. I think one could get the challenge and thrill of "observing -> hypothesizing bugs -> exploiting" across without actually making things look like this.

All in all, a good attempt but gameplay is kind of meh... For those with a little programming background, I would recommend something like "Untrusted" if you're up for a real hacking challenge.

I have a confession.

I like goofy fake hacking scenes in movies.

I know it's not indicative of "actual" hacking, and as a programmer I should probably be a little miffed at how unrealistic they make the whole thing seem. But I don't care! I love it anyway.

Hacknet promised to give me that kind of feeling, and like Uplink before it, it kinda did. It's a puzzle game where your tools are 'hacking programs' and your problems relate to breaking into computers and grabbing info, deleting info, or causing chaos.

It works well, and it reveals just how satisfying it is to solve software problems, even when it's heavily abstracted and simplified.

But my biggest problem with Hacknet is that it never really takes that next step into something greater than a simplified hacking game. Toward the end of the game there's a distinct feeling of "That was it?"

Want to hack an SSH port? Then use SSHportHack.exe. Want to hack an FTP port? Then use FTPportHack.exe. The entire game is like this. For each problem or situation there's almost always exactly one answer, and there are few opportunities to feel clever. 

In some ways the game actually feels unfinished. Many computers you hack into contain generically named folders that are either empty or have snippets of IRC conversations from Bash.org. The game is set in modern times, yet your computer only has ~800mb of RAM and you can never upgrade it. The UI for selecting systems to hack into is an absolute nightmare.

There are even mechanics that don't seem to actually...exist? For example, a big deal is made about deleting your logs and leaving no trace behind - a classic hacking trope - yet I never once saw any consequences for forgetting. I eventually just stopped clearing logs and it never was a problem

As I said, I like Hackers-style hacking. It's fun and goofy and still scratches the same itch as actual hacking. Hacknet gets close, but its far too shallow and misses the mark.

While not perfect and at times a little repetitive, this game overall is fantastic. I took my time and beat it in about 8 hours. At times I encountered small bugs or inconsistencies between programs but nothing serious enough to prevent advancement.

You've only got a handful of tools at your disposal so the puzzles aren't necessarily a challenge, but when you start trying to follow a few connected computers using clues you find on networked devices then it can get a bit challenging, but also very fun. There was only one instance where I needed to look up the solution to a problem (which seemed pretty obvious after the fact, the clues hadn't clicked for me though). 

There's a surprisingly good story given that the mechanics is hacking into seemingly unrelated computers. You will spend a good amount of time performing side missions to increase your rank within a group which can be a little repetitive but are varied enough that I didn't get bored. By the end you feel powerful in that you can break into anything if you've got a bit of patience, but even then the final mission required me to retry it three times.

Slight spoiler ahead: My favorite moment has to be when I was counter hacked (a part of the story, but might be possible to avoid) and my UI was deleted. From the terminal I was able to connect to the only other computer I could see and copy their UI files to my computer, then reboot to a different UI layout than I had before. It was a very different experience and the first time I felt truly vulnerable. I didn't realize at the time that you could change the UI so I started copying any of the ones I could find from other computers just to try them out! (you do get something that makes this easier later)

I didn't go down the Labyrinths path yet. I might start a new save to do that and get all of the tools right at the start just to play around and try to extract some more secrets that are hidden away on hard to access computers.

TL;DR: This game isn't perfect and it might not be for everyone, but it's a fun 8-10 hours and certainly different from most other games out there! It's definitely worth playing just for the unique experience!
